utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue the examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to remind you, Mr. Savkic, to -- that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I forgot yesterday to introduce Dragan Markovic, who is also assisting on our team. He is going to assist me in playing an extract of a CD later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Josse: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, when we finished yesterday I was asking about the distance between Vlasenica and Milici, and you told the Chamber -- you had told the Chamber that basically you lived in Milici. It was then very hard to get to Vlasenica. We know that you were in Vlasenica on the 14th of April for the Assembly session. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At a meeting held on the 14th of April. I don't know the number of that session, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was the next time after that that you went to the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember, but it's been quite a while since that -- it was quite a while after that. Perhaps it was about 20 days, 30, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, how did the violence break out in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The violence escalated because there were a large number of sabotages and ambushes in that period on the main roads --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop there, please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about "that period," what period exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of the period from the end of April and the whole month of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you may have mentioned sabotages and ambushes in a slightly different context, but I'm not asking you to be specific now. What do you mean by sabotages and ambushes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking of sabotages and ambushes on the main road, Vlasenica-Milici-Zvornik and Bratunac. The Milici-bauxite mine-Skelani regional road is also part of that. When we're talking of sabotage, I've already said later, sometime after May 26th, the bridge in Nova Kasaba was destroyed; it was on the main road. I mentioned that there was a sabotage in one of the tunnels on the regional roads towards the mine, and the road was blocked by tree trunks after the tunnel. However, throughout this whole period, armed formations, especially in the village of Zutica in the direction of Rudnik, were setting up barricades, cutting off roads, and hijacking the trucks that were transporting the bauxite or also they were hijacking buses with passengers in them. The most serious incident occurred on the 21st of May, I believe, when in that same village an armed formation stopped. A small TAM truck that was transporting civilians, that type of truck has a capacity of three tonnes, and it's covered -- the truck-bed is covered by tarpaulin and explosives were used. And on that occasion two women were killed, if I can recall. And also a small child -- actually, a young man of 17, 18 years old and I think also five men. That was the first time that I actually saw what the casualties look like, who were killed by explosives and massacred. I think two children and one man managed to escape from the small truck, and also a woman managed to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another serious incident took place --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. A few things. Firstly, in this period from the middle of April to, shall we say, the end of May, what were you personally doing?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was practically doing two jobs. One was to direct the security -- actually, the engineers service, wherever it was needed. For example, I was a man -- actually, the person who cleared this road after the tunnel was mined because in the JNA I served in the engineers. So this was the kind of work that I was doing, wherever it was needed, if it was necessary to check for mines or to clear the effects of mines, that's what I was doing. Because of the chaos that was already happening in that area, I was also providing advice about fortifying positions and various other engineering issues that had to do with the protection of their villages. That was actually my job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the acts of violence that you have begun to describe, how did you become aware of them? In other words, what were your sources of information at that time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw all of that with my own eyes. I've already said that. I saw the bridge in Kasaba, and I described the way in which it was destroyed. I also said that I was personally in charge of dealing with clearing the roads and clearing places where there were explosions. I used the construction machinery from the mine to clear the road. This ambush, however, in Zutica, I was the one who saw personally at the health centre in Milici when these people were brought out of the cars in which they were brought there. I saw them personally. The person who escaped, his name is Radomir Ilic, and his nickname is Kratki. He told us all that happened that day in Zutica. When we're talking about the ambush in Konjevic Polje, I think that that took place on the 26th of May. And as I said before, we continued to work as a company. We continued to transport the ore to Glinica and Birac, compared to the previous period when, depending on the time period, the trucks were going. They would be going in a column of 30 to 50 trucks. The Muslim formations, where the main organiser was the mentioned Ferid Hodzic and the already-formed military unit whose document we saw, this was the 16th Muslim Brigade, members of that brigade in Konjevic Polje set up an ambush of that convoy on its return from Zvornik when --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop there. Now, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has clarified a couple of minutes ago that what he's describing is early April until the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard evidence that a military-supported take-over of the municipality took place on the 23rd and/or the 24th of April. To better understand the testimony of this witness, I think it would be very useful to know whether when these events took place, whether that was already when armed conflict or at least take-over, however you call it, had taken place or not. Because is it what is the cause -- what's the -- what caused what? Is it -- because the testimony until now seems to -- tends to say: Well, this is what all happened. I take it that that is a -- an explanation of the situation which may make it more clear for the Chamber -- make it more easy for the Chamber to understand all the following events. But you'll understand that then we need a bit of the whole of the context for a full understanding, and that's what the Chamber wants to have, that is a full understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm more than willing to do that. I -- could I also add at this juncture how I tend to present the witness's evidence in relation to what went on during the course of the war in 1992. As has become apparent already, he has a great deal of detailed knowledge. As usual, it's difficult to disentangle whether it's first-hand, second-hand, third-hand or whatever. There are fortunately, and in the Defence's point of view, some documents which will assist, and I tend to deal with it more, I hope, by giving the Court - I use this word advisedly - a taste for what the witness has to say and his knowledge rather than going into it all, because otherwise that will take an awfully long time. But Your Honour's specific concerns I'm happy to try and turn to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savkic; before we go on and look at some specific incidents that you assert took place during the course of hostilities in 1992, the Chamber would, understandably, like you to put the description of the events that you've already mentioned into some sort of context. And to some extent, I sought to do that by asking where you physically were at this time. Where you were in military, there's no dispute, is there, that was entirely in Serb hands and under Serb control? Let's start like that.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said about the division that in Milici, before this case when power was taken over in Vlasenica, a municipality of Milici was formed without any ethnic markings or significance and it had its own Executive Board and the other required bodies. I would nevertheless like to clarify to the Presiding Judge, just to remind him that when we're talking about paramilitary organisations and arming, I said then, that as early as September 1991, especially in February and March 1992, in the village of Djile and in this other village, Zutica, there were all of these things that happened. It was exactly the same thing, the appearance of armed formations, people who stopped our workers, made them walk back, abused them, they were hijacking trucks. And this affair in the village of Zutica occurred in February and also in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what about the parts of the municipality that had, according to the protocol, been granted to the Muslims to run? Have you any idea what happened there in terms of a take-over?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're thinking of the villages that remained geographically in the municipality of Milici, I already mentioned some of them. Each incident that occurred, for example, like the one in Djile, was discussed. For example, very often the leadership --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you again. I'm going to stop you again. It's right, isn't it - I hope I'll be permitted to lead on this - that as far as you were concerned, after the protocol had been agreed upon the municipality of Vlasenica no longer existed and there were then two or three separate entities, and you have been talking only about the entity of Milici. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just talking about Milici right now, the municipality of Milici. As far as we were concerned, that was a completely legal municipality, the municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are where do you able to talk with any confidence, authority, as far as you are concerned, with what happened in what was then the municipality of Vlasenica, the municipality of Vlasenica after the 14th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I can speak only on the basis of subsequent conversations, stories, talks, mostly with Serbs but also with Muslims who returned after 1995 to Vlasenica. That's what I can talk about. I wasn't there myself any longer. The information mostly consisted of the following: After Vlasenica was taken over and the organs of power were formed in that entire area -- I'm talking about the rest of the territory now, the town of Vlasenica and the surrounding villages, I'm not talking about the Cerska enclave. So an attempt was made there to form the authorities, and this was done. The Assembly started functioning again, the Executive Board -- the new Executive Board. A few days were needed to form the public security station again because this chief, who was actually from Milici, didn't want to return up there anymore. He very quickly took over the newly formed security station in Milici. So there was an attempt and there was a successful attempt. However, in that time probably there were regretfully individuals, and this is why the last time I cited that famous writer who won the Nobel prize for literature, even though the Presiding Judge made a remark on that. But in such confusing situations like that, sometimes bad people come to the surface. And these are, as the writer says, just people who are only waiting for a situation to create more. They're not trying to contribute to a solution of the situation but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, is it my fault -- I think actually the presentation on my part could have been rather better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies to Your Honour, but this might assist. Could this be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savkic, whilst the usher does that, you must listen very carefully to the questions I'm asking you and try and answer the specific questions. I'm sure that the learned Judges appreciate that you've got a lot that you want to say, a lot of information that you want to impart to them, but it is best if you try and answer the question. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I hope you've got a pointer there. Can you point to Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you assist the witness that he points at the ELMO rather than at his screen. Mr. Savkic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's south-west a bit, isn't it, of where you are?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is to the south-east -- or rather, more to the east in relation to Vlasenica, if that's what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And point out Vlasenica town.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And very approximately could -- are you able to demonstrate with the use of the pointer where the boundary of the newly established Milici municipality was, the municipality established by the protocol of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The boundary ran from here, where I'm indicating now, through this small village of Pribinici, it encompassed the village of Vuksici, and it went through the village of Buljevici, Vandzici, Metaljka, Rogosija, and something else that's not indicated here. But when it -- where it says Sadici Donji, there is also Sadici Gornji, and then there is Korita, and then it went back down to Nedzelista, and it encompassed Tikvarici, Drakulici, Donji Zalukovik, Bakici, and then it crossed over here, across the river of Zeleni Jadar, and included this part of the territory, the place called Zagradje, and then along the boundaries of the former municipality of Vlasenica in the direction of Han Pijesak, Rogatica, Srebrenica. And basically it went all along this eastern boundary, again in the direction of the municipality of Srebrenica, and this part that I'm indicating now is the municipality of Bratunac. So that was the territory of the municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not easy for someone who reads the transcript to understand. Perhaps we ask the witness to mark this on a copy of this map during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, very good idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I've been trying to -- will you be able to demonstrate in the same manner where the boundary between the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica and the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica was?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb municipality of Vlasenica started here, from this meeting of three areas, the newly formed municipality of Milici and the municipality of Han Pijesak. And so it ran along the boundary with the municipality of Han Pijesak. And somewhere down here is the beginning of the boundary with the municipality of Kladanj. And somewhere around here the boundary with the municipality of Sekovici. And then here it encompassed the Serb villages Lukici, Simici. And then somewhere around here it crossed this creek, which has no name in fact on the map. And then it went into the town of Vlasenica. And the boundary is specifically described in the town there, and then above Vlasenica it included some Serb villages. It went in the direction of the road towards Milici, and then it turned down to this part in the direction of the river called Zeleni Jadar. So roughly speaking, it is this north-western or western part of the municipality of Vlasenica. Obviously this is the smallest part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, we will try and see whether we can get you a map and invite you, perhaps during the next break, to draw the lines on the maps so that's easier for us to understand. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take, for example, the 20th of April of 1992, you're in Milici. Were you aware of what was going on in the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said before that it was through the chief of police who obviously came every evening -- or in most cases -- well, he came to see me and we exchanged information. And we would talk to one other; we were friends after all. So it was on the basis of what they knew, the police I mean, that I knew in a way of what went on in most places, in the largest part of this enclave I mean, in the direction of Cerska because this was of essential importance to us for the transport of ore that was carried out on the road to Zvornik, as I've mentioned. And this enclave was bordering that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Chamber would like to know: Were you aware of any take-over there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I found out that on the 20th or during the night of the 21st, you mean? Yes, I did find out. After all the details that I described here last time. I found out that there was a take-over, so after a couple of days when it was all set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I summarised a few minutes ago, you, both in time and over the years, have collected information and tried to gain a greater understanding of what happened to various Serbian villages during the course of the conflict in, really, spring and summer of 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's right to say that you believe you've got a great deal of detailed knowledge in relation to that, and you could answer questions so far as some of these instances are concerned? That's right, isn't it? I'm deliberately asking you very broad questions at the moment.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can't argue about that. Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The way I'd like to deal with this is by looking at some documentation, if we can, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could the Chamber turn to tab 11. This is a report from the public security station at Milici. It's signed by Mr. Bjelanovic. Was he the chief that you were referring to a little bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you brought this particular document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get hold of it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this document, you can't see the date when it was drawn up. But it is probably a document drawn up by the police chief, probably on behalf of the centre as well. And if it was submitted to me when I was the president of the municipality, then -- well, presumably it would have been submitted to me as well, it would have been normal. And so that's a document which I must have had for quite some time. This is the period of war. The only thing I can't tell you is whether I received it before I became president of the Municipal Assembly or perhaps even earlier, I don't know. But this is one of the documents in which an attempt was made to give an expert presentation on the losses incurred, the victims, everything that happened over a certain period of time. And on the basis of the dates indicated here, you can see what period that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It might assist the Chamber if you were able to tell them, if you know, the purpose of Mr. Bjelanovic in preparing this document. Why did he prepare it; do you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know. It was drafted in order to provide an overview and in order for the prosecution and the investigation authorities to start proceedings with regard to some criminal reports. Up until that time with regard to this information, the only source of information was those who survived. And in this particular period, there was already a case -- in fact, a certain number of people had been arrested, a certain number of people who were members of military or paramilitary Muslim formations. And those people made certain statements which mostly tended to confirm what the survivors of these incidents or misfortunes, whatever, had told us. So I suppose that was the purpose. That was one point. And the other point was that the communication was being drafted already to record all the suffering and the losses on the territory of the municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to go through each of these incidents one by one. Did you -- looking at the eight different incidents that are described in this document, did you visit the site of any of them soon after they happened and see for yourself what had occurred and what the aftermath was, perhaps, more to the point?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just take a look to check what events are referred to here specifically? Yes, except for the fact that I never visited the place where the convoy of lorries in Konjevic Polje was attacked because it was not possible after that date since Muslim formations were in control of that. But I did visit all the other places. And with regard to the place called Podravanje, which was later annexed to the municipality of Milici, I was there in person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What number?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold on a sec. It's on page 5, number 8, the Muslim attack on the village of Podravanje, the mine-shaft Bracan. I was there myself throughout this attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's deal with that then. What were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of September, I was interested with the task of setting up a minefield near the mine in the direction of a canyon of some sort, since there were very few miners working in the mine and being able to ensure security there. And I got there on the 23rd, and there was a kind of depot. It was the part of the grounds that was all dug up, and I was making that minefield, and there were two security officers from the mine who were present as well. I didn't manage to finish the job that day, so I stayed at the mine overnight. And in the morning at around -- well, early in the morning, at the crack of dawn maybe, we went to finish the job. And at that moment when we started our work, an all-out attack from all sides started. Both the mine was attacked, as well as the Serb village Podravanje, which numbered more than a hundred households, and it was next to the mine. Very swiftly Muslim formations took control of the Bracan mine-shaft. It is on a hill above the central shaft Podracan. And the fighting around the rest of the mine and the village of Podravanje went on all day until nightfall. In the meantime, some security officers who were at the mine, at the Bracan mine-shaft that is, managed to come down to Podracan where we were, and they told us what went on up there, and they told us about the people who had been killed up there during the night and throughout the night. The inhabitants of the village were arriving; the village of Podravanje, I mean. The tales told were horrific. In the course of the night we noticed -- and I must stress another detail that has just come to mind. When the forces who were attacking - not just this place but many other places as well - never shouted or cried for Bosnia and Herzegovina or anything of the sort; there was always a kind of battle-cry. I mean, I can't really tell you. You really have to experience it. They had this battle-cry Allah-u-Ekber, and everybody was familiar with the meaning of that battle-cry. And the day after -- rather, in the meantime, in the course of the night, even though this whole area was in such a state, one unit managed to fight their way through and come to the central mine-shaft Podracan to join us. The day after when, together with that unit, we -- since many inhabitants of the Podravanje village had not arrived to the mine yet, we attempted to look for those locals and get them to join us in order to try and re-capture the village of Podravanje, even though that village was spread out over about a hundred square kilometres. Unfortunately, out of fear, only 18 villagers joined us. And so we were really afraid that there might be conflict amongst the inhabitants and, yeah, mostly the locals. And then at that mine-shaft Bracan, near a house which was owned by a man called Bozo, we came across two workmen -- or rather, two security officers from the mine. We could hardly recognise them because they looked like children to us from afar. And when we came close we realised why that was the case. In both cases, in their abdominal area and the area of the genitals, in a kind of circle, there were pieces of smouldering wood in the same way in which you see when you build a fire, a camping fire. So that part of their bodies was like a -- remains after a fire, and everything else also had been set on fire. We had also that in the hamlet of Nikolici six injured had been left behind. Some of those injured -- or rather, we managed to get some of the dead bodies out, but entire families had been slaughtered. One of them was the family called Marinkovic. The father, the mother, and two sons. Later on, all six of the injured people I mentioned before were found dead. I have to say that throughout that war, when we talk about formations from Srebrenica, not the others such as in the municipality of Bratunac, Vlasenica, et cetera, it was common practice to find two dead bodies, one next to the other. One body was unharmed and the other was totally massacred. And it took us a long time to realise why it was the case, and then we discovered the reason. In some cases it was very difficult for the fighters to -- for the Serbs to actually admit that sometimes they left the wounded behind, and so finally we discovered that the injured would be massacred. And those who were found dead, their bodies would not be interfered with. And once again, this mostly had to do with the formations from Srebrenica, the Srebrenica Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Savkic, I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I would have a few clarifying questions. Although, Mr. Savkic, I fully understand that it -- going back to these events makes you emotional because what you tell us is of a -- is about atrocities. Nevertheless, I would like to ask a few very simple questions. You were telling us about the village of Podravanje where you said you were, yourself, present during the attack. You also told us that Podravanje was later annexed to the municipality of Milici. When you were there, when the attack took place, Podravanje was part of what newly established municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then too Podravanje was within the newly set-up municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then what did you mean when you said that "Podravanje was later annexed to the municipality of Milici"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe I misspoke. Podravanje was before because -- no, just a moment. In the course of this period until the end of 1992 -- or rather, in this entire period, all Serb villages on the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica were burnt down, destroyed, looted, and all the population that the Muslims could possibly slaughter was slaughtered. So at the end of June 1993, apart from three smaller villages, Petrici, Kalimanici, and Crvica, all of the Serb villages, absolutely all of them, had been burnt down. So Podravanje, up until that period, the 24th, was linked to the municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I still do not understand what you meant when you said: "It was later annexed to." If you say it was later annexed to, then that suggests at an earlier moment that it was not annexed to Milici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Gentlemen, I understand. When I said "later," what I meant was when the municipality of Milici was formed, according to that division. It's easy to see from that document that Podravanje did not belong there because it was in the territory of the Srebrenica municipality. And when all these villages, the Srebrenica villages were burned and torched by the Muslim formations, then we joined that place to the municipality of Milici and all the citizens agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then do I understand you well that Podravanje was -- well, let's say in the existing system was not located on the territory of Vlasenica but was located on the territory of the municipality of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then my second question is, and I just want to make sure that I understood your testimony well, you said that you were tasked with the setting up of a minefield near the mine. Of course that's two times the word "mine," but do I understand your testimony well that you were laying mines in the fields in order to protect the mine which was perhaps part of the company you worked for? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was precise. The minefield was laid down in the part of the mine from Jadar towards the barren soil. The soil is what's left over once the ore is extracted, and that's also on the mine property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was that also on territory of Srebrenica or was the setting up the minefield, or was it in the territory of what used to be the Vlasenica municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was on the territory of the former Vlasenica municipality, because the mine was actually on the -- in the area of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The village was on the Srebrenica territory, but the mine was on Vlasenica territory? Yes. Yes, these were my questions. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We've just received a copy of the map that was being used for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask -- during the break, we'll ask the witness to -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could this tab have a number, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 11, Your Honours, will be D137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In relation to that, may I just ask you, Mr. Savkic, I see that this is a list of civilian victims which you say is prepared in order to further investigate or -- were similar lists made of any civilian victims of non-Serb nationality or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that these were preliminary actions in order for charges to be issued. So these were investigations by the relevant organs. When we're talking about the incidents in Muslim villages, I know that criminal charges were also submitted on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- no, I'm not only talking about Muslim villages. I'm also talking about non-Serb victims on Serb-controlled territory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this period, if we're still -- well, that was September. In that period, the front was already set between the Serb enclaves, if we can put it like that, and the Muslim enclaves. So that in that period, there were no such casualties other than military casualties. What I am saying is that there were criminal charges relating to incidents which occurred in May, regardless of whether we're talking about Serb or Muslim casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I then understand that this list includes Muslim victims of criminal behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list that we have here does not contain Muslim casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it's still not clear. Do you say that in this period of time in Serb-controlled territories there were no Muslim victims of criminal activities; there were only, well, let's say, victims of combat activities? Or -- it's not quite clear to me how I have to understand your testimony. And we're talking about the period -- at least this report covers late May 1992, June -- I see mid-June, September, 24th of September. It's not entirely clear to me what you say as to whether there were any non-Serb victims of what you called criminal activity during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already explained that this list was drafted after the events themselves. I also said in relation to September when I was talking about Podravan, already at that time the front had been formed and it was characterised just like in World War I by quite precise trench positions. If we're talking about later, April and May, all the individual casualties, both Muslim and Serb victims, were buried one by one. In this information -- this document does not cover them unless we're talking about victims who had been massacred. Criminal charges were issued with the prosecutor's office in relation to serious incidents, crimes, or acts. I know that criminal charges were initiated with the competent prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It still does not finally answer my question whether, if this list does not cover non-Serb victims, whether there was ever made a list of non-Serb victims that -- victims of criminal activities. So a similar list but then non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know in this context, but I know that there were relevant lists that arrived at that time. I cannot remember the sources for these lists, but they did exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to tab 11 in one moment. Could you have a quick look at tab 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could that be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 10, Your Honours, will be D138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this, Mr. Savkic, is a criminal report in relation to the incidents that you have just described in some detail. On page 2 in the English, there is a quite lengthy description of the incident. Have you any idea what happened in relation to this criminal report?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the information about what the public prosecutor's office in Vlasenica did in relation to these criminal charges. Other than taking statements from the survivors, I think that nothing more was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we go back, please, to tab 11. I want to ask you two further --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Josse, just -- I see in the criminal report Naser Oric as being the first one mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this is the same person as who was indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Actually, I think you can take it as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have not familiarised myself in detail with the charges against Mr. Oric. Is this part of the indictment against him? I'm now addressing the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I haven't made a comparison, but I have the Naser Oric indictment with me and I'll do so at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there will be -- if the OTP would have included this or similar activities by Naser Oric, then I think it doesn't need much explanation, that at least the Prosecutor admits that there are serious reasons to believe that Muslim groups -- but I see that the witness would like to tell us something. Please, Mr. Savkic, you wanted to say something to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This crime and the scale of it is definitely not -- I remember well the indictment against Naser Oric, and you may recall that what he's charged with in relation to those killed actually is a shameful thing when we're talking about this Serbian village and other Serbian villages in the broader Srebrenica municipality. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be verified. And of course, Mr. Josse, even if this attack would not be in the charges, then of course it could be -- but again, I do not familiarise myself with the content of other cases unless there's any need to do so. Of course that could shed some light on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make one observation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In fact, the Prosecution provided this document to the Defence under Rule 68. It's also fair to say that the witness provided it to the Defence some time ago. So this is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clearly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We got it from the witness. Perhaps I now realise it's been translated twice, through no fault of our own, and it's recently been disclosed under Rule 68 quite separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the two translations are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. The main reason why I was asking to see whether there's any dispute about atrocities committed by Muslim forces at approximately this time in this area. We are now talking about, by the way, about September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me go on because I'm hoping a lot of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- is not going to be in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you just two final things, one very specific and one very general about tab 11. The specific matter is the very last or the penultimate paragraph, where in fact reference is made to a tape-recording of a conversation between the said Naser and his -- Bjelanovic. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Radomir Bjelanovic, the chief, was supposed to be a witness for the Prosecution in the case against Naser Oric. Unfortunately, we're talking about a man who has a very serious heart ailment and has survived a lot of heart attacks already. He responded to the summons by the Prosecution to give a statement, but as he was giving the statement -- two attempts were made. While the statement was being taken the second time, he suffered from burst capillaries on a massive scale. I don't know exactly where. The Tribunal does have information about that. The statement is public. I listened to it. It was conveyed by radio via the mine radio stations. Some of those radio stations were on the strip-mine which were -- was captured and was looted by Muslim formations. The conversation was conducted between Naser and the chief, and it had to do with the release of a number of prisoners which the Muslim forces took with them after the attacks on Rudnik and Podravanje. They took them to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second question really relates generally to the matters contained within tab 11. As I think you've already said, many, if not all, these incidents you can give further details if asked?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It might assist the Chamber, Your Honour, and I'm sure I can lead on this. Is it -- and perhaps I should have dealt with at the start, but now's as good a time as any, if I ask the witness, as I've already said, in a leading form what in fact he did through the war, because it may not be entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right that you were a reserve officer in the JNA, and at about the 6th of April, 1992 you joined what was then or about to become the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I also said that I was performing these other tasks connected to the bauxite company. And this is what it states in my army documents, my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you were, as is clear from what you were saying about the incident you've just been describing, an engineering officer and you remained in the army till the 1st of November, 1993, when, as you've already told the Court at the beginning of your testimony, you became president of the Milici municipality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think it's also fair to say that in November of 1992 you actually became a battalion commander as opposed to an engineering officer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you one specific question, and then we will come back briefly after the break to some of the matters covered in general terms in tab 11. The specific matter relates to the Dom Kulture in Milici. What use was made of that during 1992, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was describing the situation in April and May, I already mentioned what the situation was in Milici, who passed through. So I don't want to repeat that. Milici was the last bigger settlement, predominantly Serb inhabited. Other than ten families, engineers, and craftsmen who lived in the buildings there who were Muslims, all the rest or Serbs. All of the columns when they came to Milici in the evening, after dark, because after Milici, after Nova Kasaba, as you follow the highway, there is the enclave on both sides of the road. It's the Muslim enclave on both sides of the road. People wanted to spend the night in Milici. It would happen, like it did in one case, that, for example, the cultural sports and art delegation of Serb Sarajevo were from Sarajevo - I'm now talking about April and May, that's the period before the 26th of May, before the ambush in Konjevic Polje - they would ask to spend the night. The then-president, I think his name -- of those -- I think his name was Ilija Katic. He was the president at the time of one of those Sarajevo municipalities. They were travelling so you had about 150 to 180 Sarajevans who were travelling with this programme of theirs which they wanted to present in Novi Sad. When they asked us to organise their stopover, then, for example, the women and the youth - there were also youths taking part in that programme - they were all accommodated in the houses nearby, also in the medical centre. And as for the men, we provided the -- some sort of bedrolls for them, sponges. And we accommodated them on the stage of the cultural centre in Milici, while another part of the men were taken to the school in the neighbouring village of Derventa. Before and after that, we didn't want to touch that so that whoever wanted to spend the night, if there was no room in the homes of Milici citizens, was able to sleep there. I have to say and I have to stress again that the Serb citizens as well as Muslims and Croats were still around. So there was no problem for any of them to spend the night in Serb houses, even if they were not Serbs. The next day if the situation on the roads was favourable, they would leave. So that was what the Dom Kulture was used for. In any case, there is an official who would make tours and check on the premises on behalf of the UNHCR. There is I think a record of the name of the person who would come and make these visits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. It's 10.30. Perhaps it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties perhaps try to assist me. I looked at D -- at tab 11, that's D137; tab 10, which is D138. D138 describes the Podravanje attack with 27 residents killed, as it says: "Mostly women, the elderly, and the defenders of the village." Now, perhaps you first look at the original to see -- because if it's mostly women and mostly elderly and mostly defenders of the village, then I have some difficulties in reconciling that. At the same time we have some information on it through D137. I'm especially looking at English translation pages 6 and 7 where, for example, where I would say elderly are those above 60, then at least on the basis of the date of birth you can find confirmation that at least four elderly were among those who were killed, at least in that first 13 people mentioned. The others we do not have a lot of information about their age. And to the extent we have -- I find on the second list of 12 persons, I find no one above 60. At the same time, I take it that on the basis of the first names of these persons, it should be able to identify who -- which of these persons are female. For example, I take it that Mira, for instance -- I noticed that in the course of time is if a first name ends on "a," that it's usually a female name. Sometimes we even find clues such as under 9 Mira Saric is described as "daughter." Dikosava Marinkovic is described as the wife of -- and we find some more information about Dikosava Markinkovic later in this document. I'd like to find out, and perhaps the parties could agree on -- not specifically on age, but then male or female, to see to what extent the mostly women, mostly elderly finds support in the data we find in tab 11. So if you could agree on what are typical female names and which are male names, the Chamber would like to be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm most concerned about the translation, and I'm trying to ask Mr. Karganovic to assist because it's not clear, reading the English, whether the word "mostly" applies only to the women or also the elderly and also the defenders of the village. And if it applies to all, then doesn't that, with respect, explain that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I tried to -- perhaps not clear enough. But I tried to explain that if you have mostly this and mostly that and mostly that, then you have three majorities which is difficult to get into a hundred per cent. But if you'd look at the translation, whether it's mostly -- is mainly related to women, then of course that we could then try to find -- but at least it gives us an impression of the victim population, how many women. Age, we know something about it, although not everything. And of course it does not give any information about whether people were defending the village, yes or no. So I don't have any illusion that the listing could help us on that. But you could perhaps exclude that. I would not easily consider a 70-year-old woman to be a defender of the village, although there are very courageous, elderly women. We have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, very helpfully Mr. Harmon [sic] agreed to undertake the research that Your Honour requested. So he's done it, if I may say, very meticulously, and run it by me, and he's in a position to tell the Court the results of that research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in regard to Exhibit D137 and the incident in Podravanje, the listing that appears on pages 1 -- pages 6 to 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- of D137, there are six women in the two groupings. The grouping of 1 to 13 that proceeds over pages 6 to 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that number -- on page 6, numbers 9, 10, and then on page 7, number 13 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then 2, 4 and 6 on page 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We actually ended up -- we've actually concluded that 2, 6, and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had a question mark with 9 so it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It was only 2, 6, and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Milija is not a female first name?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could ask Mr. Savkic the way I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Savkic, the first name Milija, is that a name that would be a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page is it on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last page of the -- but in general, it says "Milija Vasic."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: All three B/C/S speakers that surround me say it's usually a male name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Then that matter has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: One further matter, Your Honour, and that is we did review the Oric indictment, and the incident in Podravanje is not in that indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Are there incidents related in time approximately to this incident in the indictment? I did not review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Paragraph 27 of the indictment is informative. It states that during the period May 1992 to February 1993 there were approximately 50 Serb villages and hamlets that were burnt or otherwise destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So -- and that is presented as attacks directed against civilians, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to clarify one issue there, and that is that the municipality of Milici is not specifically named in the indictment. The municipalities where those 50 Serb villages were located are described as Bratunac, Srebrenica, and Skelani.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then it seems that this is just across the border. And at least, Mr. Josse, I understand this as the Prosecution agreeing that in that period of time in that area of the republic, large-scale, unlawful, and, I would say, fierce attacks on civilians have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can say this in terms of the Prosecution's position: Obviously all we can say is that the evidence was sufficient for the Prosecutor to file an indictment, but we can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that if you find -- if you're convinced by your own evidence, that would be a good basis for her to agree upon the matter with the Prosecution, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I would have to consult on that matter, but we wouldn't wish to stipulate to those matters because obviously the Oric case has been in process for some time subsequent to this indictment being filed. I would need to consult with the Oric team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That sounds, if not overcautious, then at least cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I'm very glad Your Honour's taken this approach because bearing in mind the question Your Honour asked before the break, it occurred to me that the Defence perhaps should ask the Prosecution to provide a huge amount of material that must be in their possession about the activities of Oric, his forces, in and around this time. And I can't imagine that this Trial Chamber wants anyone, least of all the Defence, to spend very much time on an issue that can't seriously be in dispute. So, as I say, bearing in mind the way Your Honour's put it to my learned friend, Mr. Margetts, who, understandably, has been cautious, I don't think I'm going to pursue this any further, save a small clip of a video that I'm about to play and then I'm going to turn to another aspect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And may I take it that the situation is clear that on the basis of this public knowledge, and having discussed this knowledge in court, which I find very important, because otherwise we could not hide from the parties that this has come into our minds as a Chamber, that this -- these facts which are presented in favour of the accused's case and whereas a balance of probabilities might already be enough to accept them rather than otherwise, that the probability that large-scale attacks against civilians in that area, specifically related in this document to Naser Oric, at least comes into that realm of probabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I mean, that -- in fact, again, that very thought had crossed my mind, and of course the Defence don't need to prove that matter in the same way the Prosecution do for a variety of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope that my observations, which are the Chamber's observations, are sufficient for you to -- to give proportional attention to it still needed, having heard this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savkic, the last aspect I think in relation to this that I want to deal with is you provided the Defence with two videotapes which have got a variety of material on them, and primarily both tapes present extremely unpleasant images of individuals who I think you say are Serbs, many of whom have been mutilated and massacred. That's a fair summary, isn't it, of large parts of these two videos?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is only one extract, Your Honour, that we wish to play. It's at tab 4, a short translation is found, a translation done by our own team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an interview with -- in fact, it says a pathologist. I think it's a local doctor, but we'll ask Mr. Savkic to comment upon it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what we don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say there's only one extract that we want to play, you also mean to limit that portion -- limit the introduction into evidence of that -- to that portion or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking for --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, for two reasons. First of all, the rest of it has not been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, this is, in fact, the shorter of the two videos. This one is 20 minutes long; the other is over three hours long. It's right, as the witness has already told the Court and confirmed to my question, the vast majority of these two videos simply depict dead, massacred bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then at least it is in evidence then that there exists another video which shows this. Even if we have not seen it, that testimony is still part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm happy to deal with it on that basis, if the Court is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please then proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I receive no translation. Could we stop it for a second. Do the interpreters have the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suspect that that bit may not have been transcribed, to be fair to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is -- if you say it's the first of 30 seconds, then perhaps we could agree that the first --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- because the procedure we usually follow is that one of the interpreters reads it, it's translated into French so that we also have a complete French transcript, and that the other interpreter -- because following the text is usually impossible, and that the other -- the other interpreter that checks whether what is said is the same as what we find on the transcript. The -- let's re-start from the beginning. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Who are the dead and how were they killed? "These are all Serbian soldiers from Bircani area, mostly from Vlasenica, Milici, and surrounding villages. These people were killed on a battle-field called Rogosinja, which is the local community of Cerska. This happened on the 26th in the morning, early in the morning, somewhere between 6.00 a.m. and 9.00 a.m. "How many victims were there and how were they killed? "They brought in 28 corpses and eight or nine are missing. They were either fleeing or they have not been found yet in the woods, but they are most probably dead because they didn't show up in their units yesterday. "How were the deceased killed? "Most likely -- very few of them fell into the enemy hands alive. This massacre was carried out afterwards on the deceased or wounded soldiers. This is an unheard of massacre in this area so far, but also in the history of this area and the history of the Balkans. "Some of the bodies were circumcised? "Most of them were. Also, most of them were slaughtered with an axe, their heads were chopped off, their skulls were crushed. This was an unheard of massacre, never before seen in a movie or in real life. "Thank you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, first of all, do you know what incident this doctor is referring to?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where did it take place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in a village called Rogosija in the municipality of Milici in September. I think, as the doctor said, it was on the 26th or at some point around the 26th of September. I can't really remember. And since the doctor says that there are Serb fighters, amongst those Serb fighters there were also the local villagers from on the basis of the dates of birth of the dead, and especially the locals, it is apparent that there were some elderly people there. But in order for a family to get some sort of material recognition, at that period of time most civilian victims, elderly men or women, were treated as people who had been killed in action, so as for the families to get some material recompense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the doctor being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's Dr. Djeric. He is living in Vlasenica at the moment. He's one of the surgeons at that hospital, and that's where the hospital was back then as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on whose behalf was he being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay much attention to who the interviewer was, but I know that one of the tapes that I had which was something which was recorded by an x-ray technician called Niko Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask that this have an appropriate number or numbers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D139, Your Honours. The transcript in B/C/S has not been provided, but we'll give a provisional number of D139A, and the English transcript D139A.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, in view of the character of these pictures - I'm not directly addressing the witness - but you certainly are aware that this video-clip raises some questions as to whether we are mainly dealing with murders or with -- which is, I can say for me, a similarly horrible violation of non-respect for those who have been killed in combat. That's something which does not become clear, and at least also the question of civilians, combatants, is -- at least there are some questions. I don't know whether it's possible at all to reliably resolve those matters, but rather than putting all kind of very difficult questions to the witness, I leave it up to you to what extent you would like to further clarify those matters. But it's different from burning a village, where it's clearly -- well, I would say not admitted, but cautiously said by the Prosecution that at least the charges were about wide-spread attack on the civilian population. This creates a little bit of a different picture. There are more questions related to it. I leave it up to you, but I think it's fair that you know what is in the minds of the Judges, even if they do not themselves put at this moment further questions to the witness in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I will then, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Savkic, you heard the observations of the learned Judge. Listen carefully to what I am going to ask you. Do you -- if you can, answer this yes or no. Do you have any knowledge in relation to the matters that the Bench has just raised?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the village of Rogosija on the occasion of this attack -- well, not just where these people were killed, but the entire village was razed to the ground. It was burnt down. All the cattle had been taken. So everything had been totally and utterly destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in particular, in relation to the matter of the defilement of dead bodies, do you have any first-hand knowledge of that matter, either in this incident or in any other incident?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those corpses -- well, I myself, as many other citizens of Milici, had seen them ourselves because they were taken to the health centre, that is to say the Milici hospital. And later on I saw the documents, some of which are still in my possession, the documents that came from one of the commanders, one of the Muslims who led one of the military formations, who unfortunately was exchanged and he was never held accountable. And he's still alive today. And he gave a specific description of the events, what happened, and what each and every one of the Muslim fighters did. He himself stated that there were certain wounded who were later killed, and he also named the individuals who did the killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I think this puts the -- this creates a context for the video we have just seen which clarifies in some respects that it was not just combat operation, but it was more because cattle and razing to the ground is not something you would, under normal circumstances, expect to be a military necessity. And the last portion makes clear that at least for some of the victims, this could not be considered to have taken within the limits of the law of armed conflict. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another discrete issue. Mr. Savkic, were you aware of the presence of any paramilitary units in Milici from April of 1992 onwards?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milici did not have any paramilitary formations at that time, April and May. Individual volunteers used to come, in other words, our fellow citizens who were temporarily working in Serbia, and he would go to their villages and join the village guards; or, at a later stage, they would join the legal units of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska. In one case, there were some 20 volunteers who came, and not in an organised fashion, as civilians, and -- some 20-something of them. And they came up there, and I was at the mine at the time. And when they witnessed the cruelty there, some of them left immediately, and 17 of them remained and they were under the command -- or rather, in a unit which was defending the mine. I do know that in the course of the war, on two occasions in fact, smaller units, 20 or 30 men, would come. But as soon as they realised the nature of the terrain where the battles were taking place, they left. So throughout the war these Milici units, which made up the armed forces of the Republika Srpska in the area, had no paramilitary members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next matter is this: I think at the start of your evidence you told the Chamber that the deputy to the RS Assembly from Srebrenica, in fact, was killed on the 9th of May of, 1992. His name was --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the first deputy. You then became a member of the Assembly, but you didn't take your oath until September/October of that year, when you were able to attend a session in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you some questions about your work in the Assembly in a few moments' time, but until the point that you were able to take your seat in that Assembly, how do you assess the control that the republican leadership had over the municipal leaders in Milici from the 14th of April, 1992, onwards?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically there was no influence over us because the sabotages caused us to be without electricity. Very quickly the telecommunications were cut off. And very often because of the encirclement, which went on sometimes for 12 days at the end of March, we would be completely cut off from the Serb part of the Vlasenica municipality. This would sometimes last for two days, sometimes three, but all of this was creating the difficulties that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was running the civilian side of the Milici municipality once the war started?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian side was headed by the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board of the Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, was there a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of everything that I already talked about, and since the Crisis Staff were already abolished on the 30th of May, I don't know if there was a Crisis Staff ever elected in Milici. And the fact is that the Crisis Staff in Milici never held a session or had a meeting. It wasn't operating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let's be clear, were you ever appointed to any Crisis Staff in Milici?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed if I was named a part of it. I was never informed that I was actually a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so far as the Municipal Assembly is concerned in this period, the period we're talking about, were you a member of it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, because of the well-known events that I talked about, I did not attend the sessions of the Assembly until the 1st of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the Municipal Assembly that we're talking about? That's right, yes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm talking about the Municipal Assembly. The Milici Municipal Assembly sessions from the time it was established until the 1st of November, 1993, when I became the president of the Assembly, I did not attend those sessions until then because I had other obligations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the avoidance of any doubt, you weren't on the Executive Committee either, were you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I ask a few clarifying questions. When you talk about the Municipal Assembly, you're talking about the Municipal Assembly of Milici. Milici was not the same as the previous Vlasenica municipality. How was that Assembly composed? Were people -- were elections held? Were the -- those who used to be on the Vlasenica Municipal Assembly automatically now members of the Milici Assembly? How did that work? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it exactly. At the numerous meetings when we were working on the division of the municipalities, we discussed how the Municipal Assemblies constituted -- were constituted by the legal deputies who lived in those municipalities. And then in order to increase the number of deputies we agreed that those members who were on the lists, regardless of which party who were on the lists but were not part of that particular session could be members. So all the candidates who were Serbs who were on the lists for local elections could be members or deputies of the Assembly. The Muslims from these few villages which remained as part of the municipality that I mentioned before were not included because, according to the protocol, it was possible for each village to decide - I'm talking about Muslim villages - for each village to decide which Assembly they wanted to belong to in order to implement their rights to self-government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Next question: You said you were not able to attend the Municipal Assembly meetings in Milici because you had other obligations. How frequently would they meet, even if you were not present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are records of those meetings. There are records of meetings of executive -- of the Executive Board. I couldn't really say right now, but they convened whenever the circumstances permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you any idea? Until November, three times? Ten times? Could you give an --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really couldn't say, but it was probably more than three times. Three times perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Municipal Assembly meetings are, I take it especially in those circumstances, important meetings. You said you could not attend because you had other obligations. What was so urgent that would prevent you from coming to the Assembly meetings? What kind of things I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is just one example. After the attack and the razing to the ground of Rupovo Brdo, a Serb village, which occurred on the 9th of June, and this was on the newly built road towards the mine, the mine and the village of Podravanje were cut off from Milici. The breakthrough towards the mine along this road, in order to reach the mine and the village, began sometime quite soon afterwards. I cannot remember the date. And I set out in that period as an engineer. I've already said that my duty was to demine and to check whether there were any mines laid. So -- and this is what I did. When I came to the mine I became the person in charge for defence; more precisely speaking, the commander of the mine for defence. This went on for 48 days, the work up there. So, for example, 48 -- for 48 days I didn't go back to Milici --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tell us a lot of details. I do understand that your duties as a responsible person for the security of the mines kept you away from those meetings. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, there's other one matter; I leave it up to you whether you want to take that up again. The -- I think the witness said that -- yes. The witness referred to the protocol in relation to who would be a member of which Assembly. I could not find any such thing on the protocol until now. If there is, I take it that you'll deal with the matter, not necessarily immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have overlooked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll review it and, if need be, return to the subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I just ask you to clarify this. It's probably obvious, perhaps important in the circumstances. You've told the Chamber already that the mine was a, relatively speaking, a huge concern. I think you said it employed over 3.000 people at one stage. Presumably it was of real strategic importance. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many sessions of the Republika Srpska Assembly you attended in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe three or four, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you were able to attend, to what extent did you report back to the municipal leaders in Milici what was going on at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the Assembly sessions quite often after that first session that I attended; I think I missed two before that. I was at a command post 50 to 100 metres behind the front line. Sometimes this position was on the very line itself. People would come to get me. They would inform me. I would get into the car still wearing my uniform - it was a war - to get to the place where the sessions were being held and they were held throughout Republika Srpska in that period.
