I very often had to break through, in the military sense, to get to that place. And I would follow the Assembly session, but my goal was to return to the front line as soon as possible. We mustn't forget that in this period, until the end of 1992, in this practically ethnically pure municipality, 17 villages and hamlets were razed to the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a -- both a member of the Assembly and a serving officer in the VRS, to what extent did you understand the Assembly to be telling the army what to do?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly never told the army what to do. The Assembly dealt with the matters that an Assembly should be dealing with during wartime, and they adopted the appropriate laws, adopted the appropriate decisions regulating the matters that needed to be regulated in wartime. In no period did the Assembly directly issue orders to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I noticed that in one of your previous questions, "Reporting back to the municipal leaders" was not answered. The witness more or less told us how he got to the meetings and -- but he didn't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The question I asked you a little while ago was the extent to which you reported back to the municipal leaders in Milici what you had learnt of the goings-on at the various meetings that you had attended.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would just be lightning-speed information. It would take a couple of hours, and then I would go back to my command post or when I would come usually just to spend the night and perhaps take a bath and then just carry on. The manner in which I reported back was dictated by the wartime circumstances. I would tell them what the Assembly was doing, but I would then more convey to them what the deputies were saying, also what they were talking about during the break. And we would be informed about what the situation was in all the different towns throughout Republika Srpska in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question? Why would you tell them about what was discussed during the breaks? What was the relevance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I already said, other than this first bit which would be about what the Assembly was doing, then we would -- well, these were all people who had families throughout Republika Srpska and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Many of them at the time were more interested in that kind of information, what happened to people and all these things. I mean, this was logical. It was just human nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you joined the Assembly, what was your understanding as to whether or not there was an expanded Presidency in place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I became a deputy of the National Assembly, there was no expanded Presidency. Before the Assembly session, we would meet at the so-called Deputies' Club, which included all of the parties. Of course the Assembly was not purely Serb; there were probably Montenegrin members as well. And you had people there who had doctorates, and then there were also just two deputies who only had high school education. All the others had university diplomas, academic education. So we would call the members of the Presidency sometimes for these things, but none of us were ever told of the existence of an expanded Presidency, and it didn't exist. But it's quite logical that certain things which a -- the Assembly requested to be done, then it was -- would be logical for the presidents -- the president or the vice-president of the Assembly to get in touch with people to try to seek the best possible solutions. I mean, that was to be expected, and I hope that this was the way things were done. But there was no expanded Presidency at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean exactly: [In English] "So we would call the members of the Presidency sometimes for these things and none of us were ever told of the existence of an expanded Presidency. So we would call the members of the Presidency sometimes for these things." [Interpretation] What exactly do you mean by these words, sir, that I spoke in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My words in Serbian were quite clear. If something was important and if the adoption of an important law was in question, something that was in the competency of the National Assembly, then it was logical also to hear the opinion of members of the Presidency. I'm talking about the Presidency comprised of three people: The -- I'm talking about the Presidency of Republika Srpska; I'm not talking about anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Did you -- were there any cases where one or a couple members of the Presidency actually took the floor at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you talking about the legal Assembly sessions, the sessions of the National Assembly? Yes, there were such occasions when a member of the Presidency would address the Assembly. Yes, that was quite usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But -- [In English] -- that you describe. [Interpretation] Did the members of the Presidency, did they also go to the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous answer I said it precisely. When we were talking about important things -- well, not important things, but crucial things, then the members of the Presidency would come; they were invited to the club.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could you give us examples -- or one example of topics that required the members of the Presidency to come and talk to the club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot remember now if this occurred at these few meetings in 1992. But, for example, I can remember in 1993 when the Vance-Owen Plan was being discussed, for example, that was when the -- when the president was invited to the meeting of the Deputies' Club, Mr. Radovan Karadzic was the president. And he explained why he initialled the Vance-Owen Plan in Athens. This is one example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I -- do I understand you that members of all parties would attend those meetings in the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Deputies' Club was made up of deputies from the SDS and another party -- I think the reformist party of Ante Markovic. And the deputies of the former Communist League of Mr. Durakovic and deputies of the SPO, the Serb movement or whatever the party led by Mr. Draskovic in Serbia, that's what they're called.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The Serb Renewal Movement, I think it is, says the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not able to remember the specific name, but there were two deputies from his party as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they attended all or there were no party excluded from those meetings in the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. All of them attended meetings of the Deputies' Clubs; they were members, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last answer that you gave in answer to a question that I asked was quite a long answer. Both the learned Judges have asked questions in relation to it. I've got one follow-up question. You said that: "It's quite logical that certain things the Assembly requested to be done would be logical for the president or the vice-president of the Assembly to get in touch with people to try to seek the best possible solutions." What did you mean by that, and in particular the use of the words "get in touch with people"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps "getting in touch" is the wrong way of putting it. What I meant was this: It is, I suppose, only normal that when it comes to essential matters one would want to hear the opinion of the members of the Presidency. That's the one thing. And the other thing is that in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina - I mean, there were quite a few deputies there and I was not present - but it was quite normal for certain pre-Assembly meetings or Assembly meetings to be attended by members of the Presidency. I saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understood your answer to relate to the president of the Assembly, the president of the Assembly that I'm interested in for the purposes of this question. If your answer related to the president of the republic, then that's different. Perhaps you can clarify. Did you mean the president of the Assembly or the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you to start from the beginning once again. It is not at all clear to me. Let's try and go back to your first question about this. The way I understood your question was in line with the answer I gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let me try again. I'm going to read from the transcript the follow-up question, which in itself is primarily a quote from an earlier chunk of your evidence. You said earlier -- this isn't quite word-for-word, I've cut out one or two words to try and make it simpler. It's quite logical that certain things the Assembly requested to be done would be logical for the president or the vice-president of the Assembly to get in touch with people to try to seek the best possible solutions. My first question, Mr. Savkic, is: Did you mean to say that earlier?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, once again, this part of the question refers to us, the members of the Deputies' Club, and it referred to the president or the deputy president of the National Assembly, it is only logical that they would be obliged to discuss this with us. I mean, if you meant the president or, rather, the Presidency, it was also entirely logical in the course of such work that the president of the National Assembly and the deputy, either one or the other, to consult with the Presidency in trying to find the best possible solution. The way I see it, it's quite normal. As to whether this was done or not, it's their problem; I wasn't there. I wasn't associated with them in any way, so I don't know. But I would expect that to be the case. It would be normal. From my point of view when I was the president of the Municipal Assembly, it was only normal that prior to any meetings of the Assembly I would go and talk to the president of the Executive Committee, for example, and for the two of us to agree about a number of things, as to how we could try and channel certain solutions, et cetera. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the problem was the use of the word "people." By "people," "get in touch with people," you meant members of the Deputies' Club. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you turn, please, Mr. Savkic, to tab 15. This is a document this Court is very familiar with it. It's been previously exhibited. I think it's part of P64. You've had a chance to look at it. When was the first time you saw it, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time when -- here, when I came to The Hague, in fact, when someone from the Defence team pointed him out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any such instructions circulating among municipalities in late 1991, the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any such instructions. I can give you my own personal opinion in case Your Honours would care to listen to it. But other than that, I did tell you when was the first time that I saw this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your opinion is an opinion of what? I'm not asking you to state exactly what your opinion is, but in broad terms what it is you'd be able to give an opinion about.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give my opinion on the contents of these instructions. I could give my assessment, my assessment and what I believe who drafted this document; I'm almost 100 per cent sure. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that opinion is based on what knowledge or experience, please? Personal knowledge or experience. Your knowledge or experience I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned that I'm a reserve officer in the armed forces and I graduated from that school, and my average marks were more than 9.5. And something that is striking immediately at first sight is that quite a few things in these instructions are literal quotes from various plans --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you for a moment. Well, --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness the next question, Your Honour. It's a matter for the Chamber as to whether the sufficient groundwork has been established. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- I emphasise, I don't put it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We earlier have heard questions on similarities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where this witness says that he -- at least that's how I understood his testimony, that he recognises part of the text as literally being the same to something else. You, of course, can further explore that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Savkic, I stopped you out of an abundance of caution on my part. Go on with what you were saying about similarities that you are able to draw from your reading of this document.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document is so similar -- no, I'm going to refer to individual bits of it. It resembles high school handbooks and also topics talking about armed resistance and the way in which people are meant to behave if somebody were to invade or occupy their territory. Most of these tasks more or less, if we think in terms of territorial defence, these are the kinds of references that you come across in -- well, let me limit this a little bit. But in handbooks and text-books in the former Yugoslav republics, the person who drafted this text obviously was somebody who must have worked either for the army or could have been a teacher or could have been in the reserve forces or something. I can illustrate that on the basis of many examples. The only difference is that instead of some notions in relation to the organisation of the reserve forces of territorial defence, the civilian defence, and all that, there are other notions which have to do with the representatives of the party or the existing leaders of that party. But to make a long story short, on page 3, for example, on page 3 of this document, point 6: "Strengthen the service providing security for public buildings of vital importance in the community -- in the municipality," sorry. This is something that you can come across in all kinds of plans, documents, municipal papers, high school text-books, and the like. And also point 7: "Establish control over and check the state of existing commander to reserves and proceed to," and so on and so forth. They must have copied it word-for-word from the aforementioned text-books and the like. "To step-up information and propaganda and to prepare an estimate." So items 6, 7, 8, 9, and article 11 is something that you can come across absolutely everywhere, in every territorial defence organisation manual. When it comes to civil defence, they have copied it word-for-word. "Carry out preparation, create organisational and other conditions to ensure the protection of children, pregnant women, the elderly, the sick," and so on and so forth. It was copied word-for-word from the manuals describing the code of conduct for the civil defence. And on the second level, this title which says "second level" -- well, both parts of this include similar quotes when he describes the way in which a Crisis Staff should be set up or on page 5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, we could continue but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what the witness tells us is that, to keep matters short, that everyone who would have been at high school could have drafted it. That doesn't assist very much. So if you have any specific questions on that, fine; but otherwise I think it's not of great assistance to the Chamber, apart from that you didn't need any specific knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No. I'm going to move on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I wondered, looking at this, ten pages, six times, again and again and again, could we agree on a PM, promo mori reproduction of this? Because I take it that in the course of this -- of this case, half of wood would have been saved if the 19th of December would not have been copied. At every occasion we come across it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That seems like a good idea. In general, I don't copy it, but I only -- I'll only copy it when I know the witness is going to comment on it, rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And the same would be true for what we find under tab 14 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Tab 14 I will attempt to turn our attention next to, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's a very useful lead-in. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 14, Mr. Savkic, the so-called six strategic goals. Well, we can see that these have been signed by Mr. Krajisnik prior to your becoming a deputy. When did you first become aware of the existence of the six strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived here, I mean to The Hague, that's when I was first made aware of this under this heading "strategic goals."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the existence of these goals in a broad, rather than a specific, sense?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. Even though one of the goals, which is number 2 here, it didn't go by the same name. It was not called the strategic goal as such, but -- well, if I think back, I think I know what it's all about. But at that time, nobody called this a strategic goal, but it is something else altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to deal with any of the six different matters individually. I just want you to tell the Chamber whether in your estimation these goals collectively played an important part in Serbian thinking in 1992.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that, but, if I may, I could give my own -- make my own comment in relation to these goals, considering that in the course of my work with my colleagues, deputies, I had the opportunity to get to know them very well and the way they ticked, so to say. So I think that on the basis of that knowledge I could say a great deal about the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, there's one part of the answer I did not fully understand. Mr. Savkic, you said - and you were referring to the second goal, which is: "Set up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina." You said that you think that you know what it's all about, but at that time nobody called this a strategic goal. If it was not a strategic goal, how did you consider it at that time? Was it something the -- that was important to do, to set up such a corridor but not for strategic reasons? Or how do I have to understand your answer, that you did not know this as being a strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honours, the way it is presented here, the way I knew, the way life was at the time, it was much more than a strategic or political goal. I'll try and be brief as much as I can. To give you some idea of the substance of the whole matter, on the 5th and 6th of March, the Croatian forces entered Brod, took Brod, Derventa, and Modrica. So the regular Croatian armed forces, it is a fact; we can't argue about that. And then the part around Modrica was known to be under Muslim -- or rather, Croatian control or authority. So there was no kind of communication, no links, by air, by road, by water did we have through to Krajina. And it was not possible to go through Croatia, and the world community knows --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, may I stop you here. You're describing - and least you started describing - various circumstances which I understand you deem relevant in relation to the existence of what is called a corridor. Yes. Let me just see whether I do understand you well. Are you explaining to us that it was not just a strategic goal but it was of vital importance for you to have such a corridor to exist? Is that what your conclusion would be? Or would there by any other conclusion you would like to draw from the circumstances you started to depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that's just what I was trying to say. I had just come to the true reason. The goal is presented in much the same way as the other goals. Obviously, first of all, it was a desire on the part of the deputies from different parts of the Serb republic. But what I was getting at was that it didn't have to be a strategic goal. Considering the situation - and I absolutely have to describe the situation to you - but in that situation we acted in a humane way at that particular moment in time when this was being decided. In Banja Luka we had a case of many babies who were born before the end of term, and they -- there was no oxygen to be given to these babies. And our republican authorities appealed everywhere, to the international community, to the Croatian government, through Boban, that is, through the Croatian community, that is. And I believe that they contacted the Muslims as well. And they asked for this oxygen for these babies to be provided. And nobody at the time wanted to provide this indispensable assistance, as opposed to other situations about which I'm not going to talk. And then apparently 12 such babies actually died, and the international community knew about that. But the international community did not know or did not want to know what happened to the ones who survived and what state they're in today. And had there been some goodwill at a later stage, there could have been some kind of humanitarian corridor. There could have been a water-way down the River Sava or an air corridor. Since none of that was allowed, it is the legitimate right -- I don't suppose -- I don't know whose proposal this was, but I suppose it came from the deputies, but since there was no wish to even discuss that, and there were probably discussions afterwards. But in that situation it was much more than a strategic goal; it was something that was normal to ensure links and the existence of such a corridor in the best possible way. And that corridor was manned by the regular Croatian armed forces and nobody else. And I could quote you other examples as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think your answer is clear, at least in respect to this one. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I am, partly as a result of that, going to ask you about these other goals, I hope quite shortly. I -- perhaps simplest to begin with number 6, actually. Goal 6 relates to: "Ensure access to the sea ..." As far as you were aware, was that of any importance?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska access to sea was probably the desire or the intention of the Herzegovina deputies. If we compare this point 6 and point 2, that is, well, I think that there was no need for that at the time, of course. And I really don't know how come it's here, but obviously throughout that period nobody even attempted to ensure that there was access to sea in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Goal 3, please: "Establish a corridor in the Drina River valley ..." What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that refers to my corridor, the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road or that area towards Zvornik, then there was evidently a need, our need, the need of the citizens. And it's possible that it was also a desire and the proposal of deputies who were from this area, thus to establish a corridor so that we could break out of the encirclement finally. I assume that's what it was. The second part -- well, let's just make a parallel that I just remembered. If this other part, "to eliminate the Drina as a border between Serbian state," then the third and the fourth goal: "Establish borders on the Una River," then they are contradictory to each other because here you want to eliminate a boundary towards the Serbian state of Serbia, although it never in its constitution had the term "Serb state," but a state of citizens. And then -- so how can it be that you want to have a border to one side and then on the other side, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to make a border on that side. So only on this example, I cannot really quite tell what the intention was. Obviously somebody wanted something else. The first one: "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities," it's not stated -- well, it says "borders separating," but it doesn't say independence or joining another state, but it leaves the possibility in possible negotiations for agreement to be reached on whether it would be a community of states, a majority of states. I think most of these decisions to me are like some sort of wish list, a negotiation platform to reach agreement on. None of these goals imply that they should be implemented by military means. I would just like to point out the mentality of the people whom I met, and knowing that I can assume that these were their wishes and it was a basis to talk about with the other groups. I don't think that they managed to reach an agreement, even though everything was signed in Lisbon and Sarajevo. But in view of this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, keeping in mind your question and looking at portions of the answer of the witness, what he assumes, what obviously somebody wanted, what he wants is not close anymore to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, in our submission, the answer's a useful one. The demeanour in which the witness is giving the answer is important. But, Your Honour, with respect, I'm not going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not preventing you from --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- pursue that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- If you have one or more specific questions on the matter, but it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm happy to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, apart from looking at the clock, Mr. Josse, but that's another matter. That's got nothing to do with my previous remark. Before, however, I announce the break I would like to ask one question, and otherwise it might be too far back in your mind. Several questions were asked to you about what I call the long answer on the issue of the Deputies' Club. Mr. Josse asked you some questions; Judge Hanoteau asked you some questions. It was mainly about who consulted who during the meetings of the Deputies' Club. Is my understanding correct that the president and the vice-president would consult with the deputies prior to the public meetings in order to find the right solutions? That's one. And that it also happened that the Presidency or in the example you gave to Judge Hanoteau, the president of the republic, Mr. Karadzic, would consult with the deputies. So both consultations between deputies and vice-president and president of the Assembly and consultations between members of the Assembly and the Presidency or the president of the republic, as you said, on very important matters. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably either the interpretation is bad or -- but in response to the question by the gentleman to the left of you, I literally stated: Yes, there were cases that we personally asked that the president of the republic or the Presidency come to the Assembly, to the Deputies' Club, and I gave you an example with the Vance-Owen Plan, to explain to us why the Vance-Owen Plan was initialled in Athens. That was one example that I gave. Probably I could guess. When it was a matter of extremely important questions, then we would ask for the Presidency to come so that we could hear their opinion about why they did something or why they didn't do something. But mostly this concerned important things. I don't know whether the answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly in relation to the answer he gave to your questions, Mr. Josse, it seems to be clear to me. We will have a break until 1.00 -- oh, before I go, could I ask the witness to be provided with the map of Vlasenica so that he could --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He's done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He's done it already. Thank you very much. We'll look at it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first continue the examination of the witness, then I have two matters to raise which takes approximately seven minutes at the end of this morning session. Apart from that, the witness provided us yesterday with what he said were originals of documents, which have been provided to the parties. Is there any need to keep the originals close to us or --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not as far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not, in fact, form a view on that, Your Honour. However, it wouldn't expect so, but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is there and it will take us, anyhow, until after this weekend until the examination -- the testimony will conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore if there's any need -- so the documents are returned to you, Mr. Savkic. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am - I can tell everyone - nearing the end of this examination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The map, Mr. Savkic, you've drawn some lines. It's on the ELMO. Perhaps the ELMO can be turned on. That's, I suspect, the most convenient way of dealing with the matter. Point, please, slowly to the Cyrillic proper names that you have put upon the map.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Milici, this is the approximate boundary, since I didn't have the document -- the relevant document when I was putting this in, so I wasn't perhaps specific enough, but this should be it. This is the boundary of the Milici municipality, and these are some Muslim villages which were given the opportunity to declare which of the municipalities they would like to join. Now, this is the territory of one of the part of this mine which is in the municipality of Milici or Vlasenica. And, by the way, the Presiding Judge had asked me where this minefield was supposed to be laid, and that's where I put it in, this black rectangle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop. What does the word in the bottom right-hand corner, which is in Cyrillic, say, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mine," mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this territory where I indicated SO Serb municipality of Vlasenica, and this is the boundary here. Here is the dotted line. And the entire remaining area, a part of the town of Vlasenica. And where it says "Muslim municipality of Vlasenica," this is the Muslim-held area, the Muslim municipality of Vlasenica, as well as a part of the town of Vlasenica itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A small area of dotted line in the top right-hand corner, so to speak, by a place that begins with a K, Kresani, why have you put those dotted lines in?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a Serb village. Donja Rasa, Mladinovici and Kresani. That was a Serb village, but it happened to remain within a Muslim municipality territorially speaking. And I don't really remember whether they were given the opportunity to declare which municipality they wanted to join. That's why I pointed it out, in much the same way as I pointed out the two Muslim villages within these dotted lines in the municipality of Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber asked for it. Could, exceptionally, the registrar take care of copying it for the parties and for the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break you were asked a number of questions by a number of people about the Deputies' Club. I want to ask you about Mr. Krajisnik's influence within that Deputies' Club, please. Tell the Chamber your assessment of his influence in that body.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was one of the equals in the Deputies' Club. When I say "one of the equals," and this is something that I had hinted at before, but what I meant to say is this: The Deputies' Club meetings sometimes went on for three days and three nights, and talks and exchanges of opinions would take a long time. And one of the deputies was -- had a doctorate in classic German philosophy. It was Professor Buha. And there were other people who had doctorates -- actually, all of them except for two people who only had high school diplomas. For example, Aleksa Buha got his doctorate in Heidelberg in Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. Let's try and stick to the point, Mr. Savkic. I really want you to concentrate on Mr. Krajisnik's influence, if any, within the Deputies' Club.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His influence, as I was saying -- well, the overall profile of members was such -- I mean, we were not a sect, in fact. I explained to you what -- the members there were in the club. But we would work for three days and three nights non-stop. There were all sorts of discussions, arguments being put forward. And we would voice our opinions, make suggestions, and not even a person such as the doctor in classical German philosophy could exert any influence upon us. And so of course that Mr. Krajisnik couldn't either. We felt we were all equals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have talked about the notion of an expanded Presidency. Did you actually attend any meetings of the Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was not talking about the extended Presidency; you mentioned the notion of the extended Presidency for the first time. And as far as I'm concerned, I myself never saw or never witnessed such an extended Presidency being in session or even in existence for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you ever attended a meeting of the Presidency; whether that was an expanded one or just a normal Presidency is another matter. But did you ever attend a meeting of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Presidency do you have in mind? There is the Presidency of the People's Assembly of the Republika Srpska, then the Presidency of the Republika Srpksa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. I as deputy never attended meetings of the Presidency of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then how are you able to say that Mr. Krajisnik wasn't a member of that body?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that. I had never heard of any such thing as an extended Presidency. That notion is totally unknown to me. That terminology didn't exist. When we talked to one another, the notion of extended Presidency just did not exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm returning to something which was said about a quarter of an hour ago on the meetings, rather informal from what I understood, between the Presidency and the club of deputies. I would simply like to know how you were aware or how you perceived the role of the president, Mr. Karadzic, or the vice-presidents if they were there, in these informal meetings of the club of deputies. You're telling us that Mr. Krajisnik was equally, was "our equal." I suppose that as far as the Presidency is concerned, you have an idea of the type of relationship there was between the deputies and the members of the Presidency. How did things actually happen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully democratically. The members of the Presidency could voice their views in the course of their discussions. Sometimes they did; sometimes they didn't. And let me stress once again that it was only and exclusively the club meetings that dealt with things of vital importance for the Republika Srpska. I did say that with reference to the Vance-Owen Plan, it was us, the deputies, who asked for the president of the republic to come along and explain what exactly he put his signature to -- or rather, what exactly he initialled and for what reason, and he did do that. In other situations, we could voice our views in much the same way as Mr. Koljevic and Mrs. Plavsic. For example, there were certain duties probably for different members of the Presidency. Mrs. Plavsic was mostly in charge with these humanitarian -- of these humanitarian organisations and contacts with the UN humanitarian organisations. And so that was her domain, so to say. She used to talk about that. So in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were there any instructions given by the Presidency to the deputies? There were no instructions. There were no subordination between the deputies and the Presidency, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, yes. Absolutely. They were so smart, these people, that they wouldn't allow anyone to tell them what is what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your becoming an active deputy in the autumn of 1992, did you personally know Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that we might have met going through Milici. It is indeed possible. But prior to that date, I might have seen him at a meeting -- I can't really remember what the meeting was called, but some kind of intellectuals' gathering. And I had the honour to attend that meeting, and on that occasion I saw Mr. Krajisnik. I wouldn't say that up until then we particularly knew one another. It is indeed possible that we might have come across one another on several occasions, but as to the two of us having a lengthy conversation of any sort or anything like that, up until then I have no recollection of that. When I became a deputy, I did meet him more often, obviously, at meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to deal firstly with the period prior to your becoming an active deputy in the autumn of 1992. You've described some limited dealings with Mr. Krajisnik. Presumably you read about him in newspapers, you saw him on the television. What was your estimation of him up to the point that you had personal dealings with him?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that as the then-president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I appreciated and took his work into account. I did like him and respect him, not only myself but the majority of the population. Not only Serbs, let's be quite clear, many citizens, including Muslims, in their comments always compared him and some of "their" politicians. And they would say that he was a capable man who knew how to conduct the Assembly; that was beyond dispute. I'm saying that again. Why not? I mean, he was a popular man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your estimation of him change in any way when you became a deputy?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think that we gave him too much of a hard time. I think the job with us was more difficult because of all the things that I mentioned. Work at the Deputies' Club appeared as if there were as many parties as there were delegates. We all expressed our opinions, and this is why the consultations took so long. And the situation, too, was so seriously that it was not so easy to overlook the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described his popularity. How do you assess his power in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik didn't have any power. The National Assembly of Republika Srpska at the time and in that period while it was part of Bosnia and Herzegovina and part of the National Assembly was an institution which truly had a good reputation and with their personal example, more or less, each of the deputies deserved the respect they got. And the citizens didn't look at the National Assembly in the sense that Momcilo Krajisnik personified the National Assembly; quite the contrary. I've already said that it was possible that he was more popular than the rest of us delegates were. I'm not sure in my own area whether he was more popular than I was. But I'm actually not going to say anything about myself. But he was more popular, I did say that. I don't see that he had any power. I don't see how he could have demonstrated this power at that time, in what way he could have done that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, are you ready to start the cross-examination of Mr. Savkic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Savkic, you'll now be examined by Mr. Margetts, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I could just ask if the court usher could move the ELMO so I can see Mr. Savkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, we do have a number of exhibits to distribute, and we may as well take the opportunity to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please turn the other microphone on as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the index with it, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's separate. Yes. The Chamber doesn't mind if these kind of activities are taken already during the break, the last one before we start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll keep that in mind for the next occasion. Cross-examined by Mr. Margetts:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, during the course of your examination by my learned friend, Mr. Josse, you've had the opportunity to outline to the Trial Chamber the various positions that you held that -- during the period 1991 through to the end of 1995. I'd just like to ask you: The positions you've described, both in the party, the government organs, and the military organs, was that a complete description or did you occupy additional positions that you'd like to describe to the Chamber now?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of the duties along the military line or in the organs of authority? Which functions are you thinking of?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, I think my question was very clear. I said the party, the government organs, and the military. So I'm thinking of all those bodies, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start with the party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the party. In that period, in the period sometime -- well, I really couldn't say right now when that was, whether it was in late 1991 or early -- oh, yes, yes. It could have been possibly in the beginning of 1992 when the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, an elderly gentleman, I'm talking about the Municipal Board of Vlasenica, when he was no longer able because of infirmity and old age to carry out his duties, I think that in that time -- well, I really don't know, I can't recall what time it was, that I took over the functions of the president of the Serbian Democratic Party in Vlasenica, if that's what you're thinking. The gentleman from the Defence didn't ask me that. But as soon as the municipalities were divided, I think that perhaps it had already been suspended in this period, the work of the Serbian Democratic Party, so that I really don't recall the details anymore. But I know that after in Milici the first president who was elected - or perhaps he was already elected at that time, I believe this was in 1993 - was someone else. It wasn't me because at that time I was in army. I'm talking about the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And through to the end of 1995, did you occupy any other positions in the party?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 when the work resumed, yes. From 1993 when the work resumed, yes, I was a member. I don't assume -- no, I don't assume. I was a member of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Milic, if that's a function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am still a member of the Serbian Democratic Party; I already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could you turn your mind to the government organs, and from 199 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just seek one clarification. The -- your answer was about being a member of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party in Milici. Mr. Margetts asked you: Until what time? And then you said: "I'm still a member of the Serbian Democratic Party." Would that include being a member of the Municipal Board of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Milici, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now could you please turn your mind to the government organs from 1991 through to the end of 1995. Please detail each and every government organ that you were a member of.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of any government organ, as far as I can recall. I was not a member of any government organ. You would really need to remind me, but in this period I wasn't a member of any government organ. I wasn't in the position to be a member because I was a deputy, although at that time that was something that was possible. Now that is no longer possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now in relation to military organs, from the mobilisation in 1991 through to the end of 1995, please specify each and every unit you were involved with and each and every organ of the military you were involved with for that period.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said -- I actually didn't hear the date at the beginning that you said you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, it's the same date that I've been repeating to you since I commenced this examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, Mr. Savkic didn't hear your first date. Mr. Margetts asked you this question: "From the mobilisation in 1991," and then through to the end of 1995. So we start with the mobilisation in 1991. What was your first military job or position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mobilisation in 1991, I didn't have any particular military duties except for the fact that I was deployed, if that's what you're thinking, to the joint training centre, 752, in Tuzla. That is a mixed training centre where officers train other officers primarily, if that's what you're thinking. I wasn't mobilised. That was my deployment, place of deployment. I said that I -- and it's stated in my booklet. I can't remember whether it's the 4th of April or the 6th of April, 1992, according to my booklet. And I said that I performed dual functions. One was at my company, and the other one was when I had time I worked on engineering assignments. First there was the command of the reserve battalion, so providing for their needs; and then later when this turned into a command for the whole of the town, that's what it was called, the command of the town, I still kept those duties and I was in charge of engineering duties. I did this work until the breakthrough to the mine, and I was -- had the title of Rudnik defence commander. I was there from late June until early September. And then I returned again in early September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Savkic, unfortunately I have to stop you. I don't know how long your further history will be, but we have to finish at quarter to 2.00. And as you heard at the beginning of this session, I have to deal with a few other matters as well. Well, at least cross-examination has started now. We'd like to see you back next Monday. Mr. Registrar, that would be the morning session, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In the afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's in the afternoon. We'd like to see you back next Monday, when the cross-examination will continue. We start at a quarter past 2.00 - I take it in this same courtroom - in this same courtroom. Could you -- would you please follow Madam Usher, and may I instruct you again not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given or still to be given. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to briefly deal with two matters. Perhaps first start with a never-ending story about exhibits and translation for exhibits. The Trial Chamber would like to address the parties with regard to a number of exhibits with incomplete translations. On the 15th of December, the Trial Chamber requested that both parties provide translations of a numerous quantity of their previously tendered exhibits before 15th of January, 2006. The Trial Chamber currently has still not received translations for many of these exhibits. For the Prosecution, the following delinquent exhibits remain without translations: P954, P968 to and including P973, P976 to and including P978, P992, and P1008. The following Defence exhibits are also late: That's D84, D113, D114, and D123. The Trial Chamber again requests the parties to provide translations of the mentioned exhibits, on this occasion, no later than the 10th of February. On the 15th of December, the Prosecution was also asked to verify the accuracy of the translation of certain portions of Exhibits P851, P852, and P877.A. The Trial Chamber asked the Prosecution to do so not later than the 10th of February. Since the 15th of December, there have been several additional exhibits pending translation. These are for the Prosecution: P1034, P1049, and P1050; and for the Defence: D113, D114, D123, and D127 to D129. The Trial Chamber requests the parties to provide translations of the exhibits no later than the 17th of February. I get a bit confused because on my list now I see similar numbers with different dates, but I'll continue and I'll check over the weekend whether there's any mistake. Additionally, the Chamber reminds the parties that on the 17th of January they undertook the task of submitting a B/C/S version of Exhibit D106, upon which they both agree. The version would thereafter be submitted to CLSS for translation. The exhibit submitted in conjunction with Witness Banduka was submitted on the 17th of November. The Chamber, noting the length of time that has passed since its introduction and the discussion of the parties, asks the parties to consult and to submit an agreed version no later than the 3rd of February. This about exhibits pending translation, I'll carefully check again D113, D114, et cetera. If there's any need for corrections, I'll make them early next week. The last issue I would like to raise is the following: The Chamber has carefully considered the Defence submissions on the 20th of January, 2006, regarding the progress in the presentation of the Defence case, and the Chamber would like to make some observations in that respect. On the 26th of April, 2005, the Chamber issued a Scheduling Order for the remainder of the trial, whereas the Defence had previously stated it preferred to call the accused as its first witness, at the 65 ter conference held on the 23rd of August, 2005, counsel announced that this would not be possible. On the 5th of October, 2005, the Defence filed a provisional list of witnesses accompanied by Rule 65 ter summaries. According to the estimate given on that day, the accused was expected to testify for 175 hours, that would be examination-in-chief only, on 56 different topics. The following day the Chamber, referred to the transcript beginning at 17.221, expressed its concern for the total number of hours the Defence apparently claimed for the presentation of its case, including the estimated time for the testimony of the accused. On the 15th of November, 2005, the Defence announced that the accused would testify on or at least start his testimony on the 23rd of January, 2006. On the 18th of November, three days later, the Chamber modified its previous Scheduling Order, thus giving the Defence seven more weeks for the presentation of its case. The Defence case is now due to close on the 28th of April, 2006, unless exceptional circumstances are shown. On the 20th January 2006, the Defence conveyed to the Chamber that the target date to call the accused to the witness-stand was the 20th of February, 2006. It added that it is attempting to shorten the estimated time of the accused's examination-in-chief by using Rule 89(F) and through agreed facts under Rule 65 ter (H). Finally, the Defence stated while operating, and I now quote -- Defence stated that while operating, and I quote: "On the basis that we plan the presentation of the Defence case to be complete by the currently directed date of the 28th of April, the Defence expects to call about 70 witnesses." Today, the 27th of January, 2006, the Chamber received a notification of 20 witnesses, including the accused, that the Defence now firmly intends to call. The Chamber would like to express its grave concern for the apparent impossibility of reconciling the information provided on the presentation of the case in the next weeks and the stated resolve to abide by the Scheduling Order. The Chamber has done some optimistic calculations. It started from the hypothetical assumption that the Defence will only call the 18 witnesses after the accused, identified in today's notification. From 20th of February to the 28th of April, there are effectively a maximum of 48 court days, excluding only weekends and UN holidays. That is less than 160 hours of evidence, considering the time to be spent on procedural matters and possible delays. Even assuming that the examination-in-chief of the accused will last for only 90 hours, about half of the time announced by the Defence, and assuming that the Prosecution limits its cross-examination to half of that, and assuming that the Judges do not have questions to ask, this would result in 135 hours of testimony for the accused alone. Should the other 18 witnesses take only four hours, examination-in-chief, cross-examination, questions from the Bench, their testimony would require 72 hours. Adding the 135 hours for the accused and these 72 hours, we arrive, as my staff wrote, at more than 200 hours -- yes, to be quite precise, 207 hours. That is already well beyond the time we can realistically foresee between the 20th of February and the 20th -- the 28th of April. The result of these calculations is of great concern to the Chamber. The Chamber is not in a position to fulfil its duties under Rule 73 ter (B) and (C) as one would expect it to be, that is, on the basis of the information the Rule requires the Defence to provide. The Chamber reiterates that it's therefore up to the Defence to organise the presentation of its case in the best possible way. This requires calling the most highly relevant witnesses and examining them as efficiently as possible, as the Prosecution was asked to do by the Chamber during the presentation of its case. The Chamber therefore urges the Defence to continue planning its case within the limits set, both by the Scheduling Order and by a realistic appreciation of the situation. This concludes the Chamber's remarks on the progress in the presentation of the case -- of the Defence case. This concludes our hearing for today. I should have stopped a little bit earlier because it took more time than the seven minutes I indicated. My apologies to the technicians and interpreters for that. We stand adjourned until next Monday, quarter past 2.00, in the same courtroom.
